_README: Copy to config/chains.json and fill in bridgeAddress per chain. Keys starting with _ are comments and are ignored. Run `node src/index.ts --role check --config config/chains.json` BEFORE starting a validator: it verifies every RPC, every bridge address, every EIP-712 domain separator and — with DNS — that the endpoints of each chain really are operated by different people, without touching a key.
_rpcUrls: THREE endpoints per enabled chain, from THREE operators who do not share infrastructure. This is not a failover list, it is a quorum: the validator re-reads every log from all of them and requires agreement before it signs. The floor (minAgreeingEndpoints) defaults to a majority of the PROVIDERS, so with three it is 2 — one provider can be down and this node keeps working. With two the floor is also 2, which means one provider outage stops the validator signing at all: that is why two is refused. Config also refuses any set where a single provider holds enough endpoints to meet the floor by itself, so a signature always rests on at least two operators.
_rpcUrlsAreNotAliases: Endpoints are grouped by provider, not by hostname string: every loopback spelling is one provider, and two names under one registrable domain (rpc.example.com + backup.example.com) are one provider. `--role check` additionally resolves each name and groups endpoints that share an address. That check is why https://ferminux.net/rpc is NOT listed below alongside https://rpc.ferminux.net: both resolve to <node-host>, so they are one machine and would have been one witness counted twice.
_rpcUrlsVerified: Re-verified 2026-08-20: all 31 real endpoints below were POSTed eth_chainId and all 31 answered HTTP 200 with the expected chain id (rpc.ferminux.net -> 0xf79, ethereum -> 0x1, bsc -> 0x38, polygon -> 0x89, arbitrum -> 0xa4b1, base -> 0x2105, sepolia -> 0xaa36a7, bsc-testnet -> 0x61, amoy -> 0x13882, arbitrum-sepolia -> 0x66eee, base-sepolia -> 0x14a34). Nothing was dropped this round. The two .invalid hosts on the ferminux row are NOT among those 31: they are placeholders that are MEANT to fail, see that chain's _rpcNotes. Public endpoints are rate-limited, change hands and disappear; re-run `--role check` before you rely on them, and prefer your own node as one of the three wherever you can run one.
_confirmations: Reorg budget per chain. The rule: wait long enough that reversing the source block costs more than the transfer is worth. See README.md#reorg-budgets for the full reasoning; the short version is in each chain's _notes. `confirmations` is a FLOOR under every finality mode below and is never lowered by any of them.
_finality: Per-chain `finality` block, README.md#finality-modes. A block COUNT is the wrong primitive on a chain without a finality gadget: on PoW the block time swings with hashrate (the 2026-08-21 stall left the bridge on 'Confirming 12/64' for hours), and on an authority chain a reorg costs zero work at any depth. So the mode is explicit: `count` (chains with a real finality tag: BSC, Ethereum, the L2s), `work-and-time` (PoW: accumulated difficulty above the block >= workThreshold AND wall clock >= timeFloorMs), or `checkpoint` (authority chains: the signed CheckpointRegistry on BSC is the SOLE finality source). Under work-and-time and checkpoint a PACE monitor runs: when the median of the last `pace.window` block gaps exceeds `pace.degradedFactor` x `pace.targetBlockTimeMs`, or no block has arrived for `pace.stallAfterMs`, the chain is DEGRADED, the validator REFUSES to sign, and /status says 'producing blocks slowly; transfers are paused until it recovers' with the measurement. A `checkpoint` registry, when configured, is enforced in EVERY mode: the validator will not sign a transfer whose source block is above the latest attested checkpoint, refuses if the attested hash differs from what it sees at that height on Ferminux (that is a detected reorg), and refuses if the checkpoint is older than `maxAgeMs`. It cannot read the registry -> it does not sign. Publish checkpoints with bridge/ops/checkpoint.sh.

chains.name: ferminux
chains._notes: Ethash PoW, ~7s blocks, no finality gadget. Reorg depth is bounded by hashrate, not by protocol, and Ferminux hashrate is small — so this is the DEEPEST wait in the set, not the shallowest. 64 blocks is ~7.5 minutes. Do not lower it because the chain 'feels' fast: a 51%-capable miner rewriting 10 blocks costs almost nothing here, and rewriting 64 costs 6.4x that.
chains._rpcNotes: There is exactly ONE public Ferminux RPC operator, and it is us — so two of the three witnesses on the home chain have to be nodes you control or nodes a counterparty controls. The two .invalid placeholders below are deliberately unresolvable: `--role check` fails on them, which is the point. Replace them with real hosts before setting enabled=true. Running your own Ferminux node is a small ask (geth fork, ~7s blocks) and it is the only endpoint in this file nobody else can take away from you.
chains._finality: BEFORE the Clique fork: work-and-time. workThreshold is total difficulty in the chain's own units, summed over the blocks ABOVE the source block. Measured live 2026-08-21 through all three RPCs at head 20744: 81 blocks carried 98,893,866,925 of work, i.e. ~1.22e9 per block, so 64 blocks' worth is ~7.8e10 — that is the value below. It MUST be re-derived when hashrate moves materially (cast block latest --rpc-url https://rpc.ferminux.net, field `difficulty`, times 64): too low and the time floor does all the work, too high and the bridge waits longer than intended. timeFloorMs 450000 = 7.5 min, the wall clock 64 blocks were meant to be. Pace measured the same day: median gap 14s, max 63s, against the 7s target — already 2x nominal, which is why degradedFactor is 4 and not 2; the stall rule (no block for 300s) catches the 2026-08-21 failure mode outright. AFTER the fork: set mode to "checkpoint", delete workThreshold/timeFloorMs (they are refused outside work-and-time), keep pace, and set pace.targetBlockTimeMs to the Clique period. The checkpoint block is included in BOTH modes: it is the only defence that prices a zero-cost reorg, so it goes live before the fork, not after. registryChainId 56 means the registry is read through the bsc row's 3-provider quorum, so that row must be enabled.

checkpoint._note: CheckpointRegistry on BSC (chain 56), owned by the BSC multisig 0x15D0791d49A089863243BE2C2050e5d26E1bBA9c. Deploy with `forge create src/CheckpointRegistry.sol:CheckpointRegistry --constructor-args 0x15D0791d49A089863243BE2C2050e5d26E1bBA9c`, then fill registryAddress in here and in CKPT_REGISTRY for ops/checkpoint.sh. maxAgeMs 21600000 = 6h: publish at least every shift, or the bridge pauses itself — which is the intended failure.

limits._note: Local validator caps, in the token's smallest unit. These are a SECOND fence inside the contract's caps — set them at or below what registerCanonical/registerWrapped used. Tightening here is instant and needs no timelock.

0x00000000000000000000000000000000000000._note: FMX, the native coin. 25,000 per transfer / 100,000 per rolling 24h.

chains.name: ethereum
chains._notes: PoS with real finality. Prefer the tag over a block count: `finalized` is two justified epochs, ~13 minutes, and is economically final (reverting it burns a third of the staked supply). The 32-block count is only the floor applied while a node has not caught up enough to serve the tag.
chains._rpcNotes: Allnodes (publicnode), dRPC and Cloudflare — three unrelated operators on three networks. rpc.ankr.com/eth was here and now answers 'Unauthorized: you must authenticate with an API key'; eth.llamarpc.com answers 521. Both were dead weight in the quorum, which is exactly the failure this list is supposed to survive.

chains.name: bsc
chains._notes: 3s blocks, 21 validators, BEP-126 fast finality (~2-3 blocks once 2/3 have voted). `finalized` is served and is the real safety line; 20 blocks (~60s) is the fallback floor. BSC has had multi-block reorgs before fast finality, which is why the floor is not 3.
chains._rpcNotes: Allnodes, the Binance-operated dataseed, and 1RPC (Automata). bsc-dataseed1.binance.org still answers but bnbchain.org is the current name for the same fleet — listing both would be one provider twice, so only one is here.

chains.name: polygon
chains._notes: Bor produces ~2s blocks that are NOT final until Heimdall milestones them. Bor reorgs of well over 100 blocks have happened in production. 128 blocks (~4.5 min) is the floor and `finalized` (milestone-backed, ~16 blocks post-Napoli) is the real line. This is the chain where a small confirmation count has actually cost bridges money.
chains._rpcNotes: polygon-rpc.com — the endpoint every Polygon doc still prints, and the one this file used to ship — now answers 'API key disabled, tenant disabled' with HTTP 403. Replaced by dRPC and 1RPC alongside Allnodes.

chains.name: arbitrum
chains._notes: L2. The sequencer does not reorg in normal operation, so a block count here measures almost nothing — the real risk is an L1 reorg rewriting the batch that contained the block. Use `finalized`, which on Arbitrum tracks L1 finality (~15 min). 300 blocks (~75s at 0.25s) is only a floor. maxBlockRange is larger because blocks are tiny and frequent.

chains.name: base
chains._notes: OP-stack L2, 2s blocks, same L1-derived finality argument as Arbitrum. `finalized` follows L1 (~15 min). 180 blocks (~6 min) is the floor for the window where a block is sequenced but the L1 batch is not yet final.

chains.name: sepolia
chains._notes: Ethereum testnet. Same finality mechanics as mainnet, much less economic weight behind them — treat testnet money as free and testnet confirmations as advisory.
chains._rpcNotes: rpc.sepolia.org now serves an Apache 404 and sepolia.drpc.org is paid-plan only, so both were dropped. Allnodes, 1RPC and Tenderly answer.

chains.name: polygon-amoy
chains._rpcNotes: rpc-amoy.polygon.technology no longer resolves at all (NXDOMAIN) — a dead name in a quorum list is an endpoint that can never disagree with anything. Replaced by dRPC and Tenderly.

http._note: Bind to a private interface. /health is unauthenticated by design; EVERYTHING else needs the bearer token. An empty apiToken means no authentication at all, so it is only accepted on a loopback bind — any other host is a startup failure, because /status and /transfers describe every in-flight transfer, sender and recipient included. Generate one with: openssl rand -hex 32. Put TLS in front of this (nginx/caddy) — validators talk to each other over the public internet in a multi-party deployment.
http._rateLimit: Per-client-IP token bucket applied to every route including /health, so an unauthenticated caller cannot spend this process's CPU and sockets keeping a validator from answering the submitter. burst is the back-to-back allowance, refillPerSecond the sustained rate.

keystore._note: Never put a private key in this file. `--role keygen --out <path>` writes an encrypted V3 keystore at mode 0400; the password lives in its own 0400 file, ideally on a different volume or injected by systemd credentials.

transport._note: http = multi-party (each validator on its own host, its own custodian). shared-dir = single-operator convenience: it is NOT M-of-N security, because one operator who can write that directory can write every file in it.

validator._note: requireRpcQuorum: EVERY healthy endpoint must show the same log before this node signs. Setting it to false is refused unless insecure.allowPartialEndpointAgreement is set with the acknowledgement sentence.
validator._floor: Independent of this flag, each chain has a minAgreeingEndpoints floor (default: a majority of its PROVIDERS, never below 2, and never satisfiable by one provider on its own). A validator that cannot reach that floor REFUSES — it never falls back to trusting the one endpoint still answering, because 'the one endpoint still answering' is what an eclipse attack arranges.
